blogs.title: Intrinsic Evidence, Not 404(b): The Eighth Circuit’s Broad Admissibility Rule for Prior Gun Possession
blogs.description: The panel leaned on its well-worn intrinsic-evidence doctrine to admit testimony that witnesses had seen the same sawed-off rifle in Justin Cutbank’s hands before the charged incident. This post unpacks how the Eighth Circuit treats prior possession of the same firearm as intrinsic—thereby bypassing Rule 404(b)’s propensity limits and notice requirements—and contrasts that approach with circuits that have narrowed or criticized the ‘inextricably intertwined’ label. We explore Battle’s continuing force in firearm-possession prosecutions, the modest role Rule 403 played here, and practical takeaways for defense counsel seeking to cabin ‘continuous possession’ proofs. The result reinforces a prosecution-friendly path to proving dominion and control over the exact weapon at issue.

blogs.title: From Gall to Goodhouse: Stacking Enhancements and the Presumption of Reasonableness in ACCA Sentencing
blogs.description: Cutbank’s 292-month sentence sits at the bottom of a guideline range buoyed by multiple enhancements: the NFA-style weapon base level, obliterated serial number, reckless endangerment during flight, and—most controversially—§ 2K2.1(b)(6)(B)’s ‘in connection with another felony offense.’ This post walks through how the district court’s reliance on unobjected PSR facts sustained the four-level § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B) bump, how § 4B1.4’s ‘greater offense level applies’ rule interacts with ACCA, and why the Eighth Circuit’s presumption of reasonableness for within-range sentences leaves little room for § 3553(a) ‘parsimony’ arguments. We also consider recurring ‘double counting’ concerns in firearms cases and offer strategic guidance on preserving factual and legal objections to the “another felony” finding at sentencing.

blogs.title: Hearsay, Confrontation, and Cross-Examination Pitfalls: The Eighth Circuit’s Practical Evidentiary Playbook
blogs.description: On appeal, Cutbank challenged the admission of context-driven officer testimony, the timing (and necessity) of limiting instructions, and a witness’s reference to a family member’s death by gun—all rebuffed under a deferential abuse-of-discretion standard and harmless-error backstop. This post analyzes the court’s application of Bennett and Charboneau to conclude that contemporaneous limiting instructions were unnecessary and the Confrontation Clause satisfied once the declarant testified. We also examine the court’s insistence on authenticating police reports used for impeachment under Cumbie, and the Rule 403 handling of emotionally charged testimony elicited during cross. The opinion’s reminder to the government not to broaden issues on appeal doubles as a practice note for both sides on clean appellate issue framing.

blogs.title: ACCA After Erlinger: Jury Findings and the Eighth Circuit’s Streamlined Review
blogs.description: The panel notes that the jury found Cutbank had three or more prior violent felonies, a posture consistent with post-Erlinger practice of submitting ACCA-triggering facts (at least the ‘different occasions’ question) to the jury. This post situates Cutbank within that developing landscape: what must juries find, what may judges find, and how PSR-adopted facts can still drive guideline enhancements like § 2K2.1(b)(6)(B). We highlight open questions about the scope of jury determinations after Erlinger and the limited appellate scrutiny when the sentencing court correctly calculates the range and gestures to § 3553(a). For practitioners, the case underscores the importance of clearly delineating which ACCA facts are jury issues and building a record that resists overreliance on unobjected PSR narratives.
